comparator.name: Bachelor Applied Physics
comparator.sourceNotes: TU Delft's current programme page, checked 2026-10-03, describes a three-year Applied Physics bachelor organised around classical mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism and quantum mechanics, with one physics course, one mathematics course and a laboratory or project in each quarter of year one and two theory courses plus a laboratory or project in each quarter of year two. Its linked official curriculum chart was created in August 2026 and is marked September 2026. The chart supplies the course-level allocation of the complete 180-EC programme. Year three contains a 30-EC minor, two 5-EC electives, 5 EC of Critical Reflection on Science and Argumentation, and a 15-EC individual Bachelor Final Project.
components: Advanced Linear Algebra and Differential Equations
Year 2, quarter 2 mathematics and physics course.
Year 3, semester 1 free-choice broadening or deepening minor, which may be completed abroad.
Critical Reflection on Science and Argumentation
Ten-week individual full-time research project in a TU Delft research group.

core: Fundamental and applied physics, experimental laboratories, precision measurement, materials, devices and instrumentation
Calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, numerical methods, probability, signals and physical-system models
Scientific programming, data analysis, image processing, algorithms and computational prediction
Technical-system design, sensing, product development and technological innovation
adjacent: Renewable-energy technologies, natural physical systems and sustainable resource applications
Medical technologies, imaging and quantitative study of living systems
Advanced materials, optics, quantum-device principles, nanoscale systems and nanotechnology
questions: How can mathematical and computational models describe and predict complex physical or living systems?
How can physical principles and quantitative evidence inform technical, energy and medical applications?

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, autonomous systems & energy technology
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is dominated by mathematics, programming, algorithms, data, imaging, optimisation, machine learning and robotics, with a bounded energy-technology strand. It does not claim mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum, materials, device, instrumentation or experimental-physics formation.
alternatives.concept: Develop calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, linear systems, probability, programming, algorithms, image analysis, optimisation, machine learning, robotics and autonomous decision methods, with a renewable-energy technology strand. This is a computational related-fields response, not Applied Physics equivalence.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and nine level-300 courses. Programming precedes algorithms and autonomous-system work; Mathematical Methods precedes dependent mathematics, robotics and neural networks; Sustainability Essentials I precedes II and Renewable System Design. Every formal prerequisite occurs earlier and every course is offered in its assigned Fall 2026 cohort term.

alternatives.label: Mathematical modelling, Earth systems & sustainable technology
alternatives.labelReason: Six Earth and environmental courses replace six specialist algorithmic courses, producing a natural-system, resource and energy curriculum while keeping quantitative modelling central. The label does not imply geophysics or Applied Physics equivalence.
alternatives.concept: Combine mathematical and computational models with Earth-system science, geospatial and laboratory investigation, water–mineral interactions, resource recovery, climate mitigation and renewable-system assessment to study natural physical systems and sustainable technologies. This remains a related-fields route rather than an Applied Physics curriculum.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and eight level-300 courses. Sustainability Essentials I precedes II and all dependent resource and energy courses; Mathematical Methods precedes later mathematics, robotics and neural-network study. Every formal prerequisite occurs earlier and every course is offered in its assigned Fall 2026 cohort term.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses, or 45 EC, differ in each direction. Optimisation, computer networks, algorithms, advanced algorithms, AI decision-making and reinforcement learning are replaced by Earth-system modelling, Dynamic Earth, soils and aquifers, environmental biogeochemistry, resource recovery and advanced resource research. These changes implement a natural physical-systems direction rather than threshold-filling substitutions.

alternatives.label: Biomedical systems, imaging & quantitative modelling
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum contains a sustained molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease-science core alongside mathematics, programming, imaging and data modelling. It does not claim medical physics, physical instrumentation or professional clinical preparation.
alternatives.concept: Study living and human systems through molecular biology, physiology, neurobiology, laboratory work and disease mechanisms, combined with calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, signals, probability, programming, machine learning and image analysis. This responds to medical-technology and imaging evidence through related fields, not a Medical Physics or Applied Physics curriculum.
progression: The schedule contains 24 unique courses, Personal & Professional Development in Year 1 and seven level-300 courses. Life-science, biomedical and brain foundations precede dependent molecular, anatomical, physiological, disease and cognitive courses; Mathematical Methods precedes advanced quantitative work. Every formal prerequisite occurs earlier and every course is offered in its assigned Fall 2026 cohort term.
alternatives.distinctness: Against the autonomous-systems route, fourteen courses (105 EC) differ in each direction; against the Earth-and-energy route, thirteen courses (97.5 EC) differ in each direction. The third programme replaces most specialist algorithms, autonomy, Earth, resource and energy study with molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease science, as required by the medical-technology direction.

candidates.label: Natural physical systems, resources and renewable energy
Medical technologies, imaging and living systems
Quantum, optical, materials and nanoscale technology
candidates.reason: UCR has sustainability materials context and resource-recovery applications, but no quantum, optics, condensed-matter, materials-physics, device-physics, nanofabrication or experimental-characterisation sequence from which a coherent 24-course programme could be built.

selection.assessment: The first programme is the strongest related quantitative and computational systems response. The renewable-energy and medical-technology evidence each supports a coherent and materially different complete route, and all three programmes pass the pairwise distinctness floor. The maximum of three alternatives is therefore reached; the separate quantum, optical, materials and nanotechnology direction remains infeasible because UCR lacks its disciplinary and experimental sequence.

blocks: Both support computational scientific work; UCR teaches general programming rather than a physics-specific computational-science sequence.
Both establish calculus for quantitative models; UCR also introduces matrices, complex numbers and differential equations.
Both directly study linear algebra, matrices, vector spaces and transformations.
Both address differential equations and computational solution methods; UCR emphasises general numerical analysis rather than physics-specific modelling.
Both extend calculus to multivariable settings; UCR also covers complex functions and differential equations.
Both use linear-system, transfer-function and signal representations; UCR remains mathematical rather than an electronics or instrumentation course.
Both develop probability and statistical modelling; UCR does not provide statistical physics.
The 15-EC individual Applied Physics research project has no scheduled UCR equivalent; optional UCR independent research is comparison-only.

notes.text: The UCR programmes develop mathematical and computational models, autonomous systems, natural-system and renewable-energy analysis, and biomedical imaging and data perspectives. They do not reproduce mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, waves, quantum or statistical physics, solid-state and materials physics, circuits and electronics, precision instrumentation, cumulative physics laboratories, staged physics-design projects or the Applied Physics research project.
